Bias in genome-wide association test statistics due to omitted
interactions
Burak Y elmen1,*, Merve Nur G¨ uler1, Estonian Biobank Research T eam 1, T˜ onu Kollo2,
M¨ art M¨ ols2, Guillaume Charpiat 3, Flora Jay 3
1 Estonian Genome Centre, Institute of Genomics, University of Tartu, Tartu, Estonia
2 Institute of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Tartu, Tartu, Estonia
3 CNRS, INRIA, LISN, Paris-Saclay University, Orsay, France
*burak.yelmen@ut.ee
Abstract
Over the past two decades, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) enabled the discovery of thousands
of variants associated with many complex human traits. However, conventional GWAS are still widely
performed with linear models with the assumption that the genetic effects are predominantly additive.
In this work, we investigate the test statistic behavior when linear models are used to obtain significant
genotype-phenotype associations without accounting for epistasis. We first algebraically derive mean
and variance shift in the null statistic due to the omitted interaction term, and define the boundary
between conservative (i.e., deflated statistic tail) and anti-conservative (i.e., inflated statistic tail) regimes
for the common GWAS significance threshold. We then perform phenotype simulation analyses using
the Estonian Biobank genotypes and validate the mathematical model. We demonstrate that the anti-
conservative regime is plausible under realistic parameter settings and models omitting interaction terms
can produce spurious significance. Our findings suggest caution when interpreting statistically significant
signals reported in the literature based on linear models, especially for large-scale GWAS.
Keywords:genome-wide association studies, epistasis, complex traits, linear mixed models

Introduction 1
Biological systems consist of multiple interrelated components, which makes them difficult to model 2
faithfully using linear functions. It is reasonable to assume that the relationship between genetics and 3
complex traits exhibits similar complexity. Indeed, multiple studies have proposed epistasis and gene- 4
environment interactions as fundamental causal mechanisms of phenotypic variance [1–3]. Genome-wide 5
association studies (GWAS), despite allowing the discovery of thousands of genotype-phenotype links 6
with functional importance, are still widely performed with linear models after almost two decades 7
[4]. This prevailing methodological trend might be attributed to multiple factors such as the ease of 8
interpretability, attainable computational requirements, tradition and studies suggesting that the genetic 9
component of phenotypic variance can mainly be explained by additive models [5–7]. 10
This assumption of mainly additive effects, however, may hinder the efforts to understand the causal 11
genetic mechanisms since the true associations might be nonlinear, despite being captured without 12
nonlinear modeling [8]. Even if we accept the mainly additive model for association discovery, recent 13
methods point to large variability of non-additive variance (i.e., the left-over variance after accounting for 14
additive variance) among phenotypes [9]. In this light, various works have either tried to approach GWAS 15
with nonlinear models such as neural networks [10, 11] or explicitly infer/integrate epistasis [12–14]. 16
There are some hints in the literature on the consequences of omitting interaction terms in GWAS. 17
Omitted variable bias, which is the bias in model-estimated coefficients due to the exclusion of variables 18
relevant to the response variable, is a well known statistical concept [15] and it has been used to 19
demonstrate that GWAS summary statistics might tag non-additive variance whenever there is nonzero 20
correlation between genotypes and the interaction terms [9]. Furthermore, some evidence was presented 21
in a recent study for “synthetic associations” (i.e., associations due to combined effects of multiple other 22
variants [16, 17]) due to epistasis [18]. Interestingly and perhaps alarmingly, it was suggested that 3-5% 23
of GWAS Catalog peaks might be synthetic, but the findings were obtained from indirect evidence based 24
on unusual linkage disequilibrium (LD) patterns and did not necessarily point to spurious associations 25
due to epistasis. Here we use “spurious” to refer to associations arising purely due to epistasis which 26
does not include the target SNP. To the best of our knowledge, the effects of omitting interaction terms 27
in GWAS have not been modeled to understand whether this omission can result in spuriously significant 28
associations under realistic settings. 29
In this work, we derive a mathematical model to assess the effects of omitted interaction terms on 30
GWAS test statistics. We initially define a true data generating process (DGP) for a phenotype with a 31
fixed interaction component. Our mathematical setup is that a standard linear mixed model (LMM) is 32
fitted for this phenotype to estimate the target SNP coefficient α. We preprocess all vectors from the 33
true DGP and the fitted model to whiten and remove covariate effects. Based on the equality of the 34
phenotype value for both models after preprocessing, we derive ordinary least squares (OLS) estimates 35
for the expected value of the estimated ˆα and its variance, under the null hypothesis α = 0. These allow 36
us to derive the mean and variance of the true null statistic as opposed to the nominal null N (0, 1). We 37
then define the R(x) conservativeness ratio of true to nominal p-value to assess anti-conservative and 38
conservative regimes for a given critical value x. To ensure that both the SNP and interaction effects are 39
clearly defined, we introduce an extended null concept, strict no-path null, in which not only the target 40
SNP coefficient is 0, but also the target SNP cannot be part of the interaction features. Intuitively, this 41
makes sure that any identified bias of the test statistics is purely due to the realized interaction component 42
and its correlation with the target SNP. Using this strict null concept, we simulate two sets of 10,000 43
phenotypes based on the Estonian Biobank genotype dataset [19] with varying non-additive variance 44
fraction estimates from the literature, use REGENIE [20] to obtain summary statistics for target SNPs and 45
confirm the mathematical model. Both the mathematical model and the simulation results demonstrate 46
that even under minimalistic non-additive variance estimates and low correlation between the target SNP 47
and the interaction component, anti-conservative regime is plausible and multiple non-associated SNPs 48
are identified as significant due to the omitted interaction term. The key interpretation of our findings is 49
that widely used linear models which do not compensate for epistatic effects can be prone to identifying 50
spurious associations, especially when the sample size is large. 51

Discussion 204
In this work, we derived a mathematical model characterizing the test statistic bias in GWAS if the 205
true genetic architecture involves epistasis which is not taken into account in the fitted linear model. 206
The inflationary bias at the extreme tail is mainly driven by the positive shift in the mean of the null 207
statistic, whereas the downward shift in the variance drives deflation, yet the dominant tendency for the 208
critical t-statistic value ±5.45 (corresponding to the common GWAS significance p-value 5e-8) is inflation 209
(hence, increased spurious significance) under a vast range of realistic parameter values (Fig 2, 3). We 210
were able to define the mean and variance shift in terms of three terms: (i) λ, the variance fraction of 211
the interaction component, (ii) ρ, the correlation between the target SNP and the realized interaction 212
term, and (iii) n, the sample size. For the range of λ, we used the estimations from literature [7]. For 213
the range of ρ, we first derived a maximum threshold algebraically without needing the interaction term 214
coefficients. We also performed phenotype simulations with the full interaction architecture. As expected, 215
even under the strict no-path null, absolute value of ρ can be high due to LD between the target SNP 216
and the interaction SNPs. Interestingly, even when the target SNP and the interaction SNPs are on 217
different chromosomes, ρ can reach sufficient non-zero values to produce spurious significance (Fig 1, 2). 218
Another interesting observation was that the problem of spurious significance is positively correlated 219
with the sample size. Average sample size for GWAS in 2022 was reported to be up to 140,000 [4]. It is 220
now also not uncommon to utilize more than a million sample-sized datasets thanks to large biobanks 221
[22]. As the sample size reaches a million, even minimal estimates for the interaction variance fraction 222
λ (e.g., ∼ 0.03) and correlation ρ (e.g., ∼ 0.03) can result in ptrue(x = ±5.45) ⪆ 0.5 regime where we 223
expect approximately half of the statistically significant hits to be spurious (Fig 2). 224
One of the limitations of our model is the initial assumption of perfectly estimated V excluding u, 225
which we mainly proposed to be able to equate true and misspecified model’s phenotype vectors. This is 226
not realistic because the structured part of the estimated ˆV could potentially capture some variation 227
from the interaction term. This effect heavily depends on how well the kinship matrix and polygenic 228
variance estimations are affected by the unrealized true interaction structure. In other words, it depends 229
on how much of the variance from the true interaction term is modeled under the non-genetic variance 230
component of the estimated ˆV . Modern LMMs generally estimate kinship matrix K and variance of the 231
polygenic effect σ2
η with the leave-one-chromosome-out (LOCO) method in which the chromosome of 232
the target SNP is removed from the estimation to avoid proximal contamination. This means that our 233
model’s limitation could especially be relevant if the target SNP and interaction SNPs are on different 234
chromosomes, but the most severe bias where the target SNP and interaction SNPs are on the same 235
chromosome most likely persists even when the u interaction space partially aligns with K. Indeed, we 236
were able to confirm via LMM-based GWAS on simulated phenotypes that our mathematical model is 237
consistent (Fig 4). 238
As a precautionary check for spurious significance without the omitted term, for each simulated 239
phenotype, we also simulated a version for which the only difference is the subtraction of the realized 240
interaction component from the final phenotype. We detected 4 and 2 spurious associations (i.e., p-val 241
>5e-8) over 38,340,000 tested SNPs in 10,000 simulated phenotypes for n = 100, 000 and n = 210, 145 242
datasets, respectively. In contrast, for phenotypes with the interaction term, 1851 and 6076 spuriously 243
significant SNPs were detected for n = 100, 000 and n = 210, 145 datasets, respectively. 244
Another limitation of our model is that true ρ cannot be obtained without knowing the true interaction 245
architecture. We assessed ρmax estimates over interaction matrices with higher-order terms and observed 246
that mean ρmax estimates are consistent but extreme ρ values might be less likely with higher-order 247
products (see Appendix B). This is still not sufficient to deduce meaningful conclusions on the range of 248
the ρ parameter since the true interaction terms might be defined by a multitude of different nonlinear 249
functions. Without more precise estimates for the range of ρ, it is not trivial to transform our model 250
into a diagnostic framework in real GWAS. However, since ρ can reach sufficiently high values even 251
when the target SNP and interaction SNPs (from two-way to ten-way, see Appendix B) are on different 252
chromosomes, it is reasonable to assume that real GWAS is affected by this bias. We leave investigating 253
the extent of this bias and developing diagnostic frameworks to future work.254
GWAS are crucial for providing the basis of functional studies which are required to understand the 255

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import norm
import os

n = 100_000
x = 5.45

rho_vals = np.linspace(-0.3, 0.3, 400)
lambda_vals = np.linspace(0, 0.171, 400)

RHO, LAMBDA = np.meshgrid(rho_vals, lambda_vals)

# Model formulas
MU = (RHO * np.sqrt(LAMBDA * n)) / np.sqrt(1 - LAMBDA * RHO**2)
SIGMA = np.sqrt((1 - LAMBDA * RHO**2) / (1 - LAMBDA))
alpha_t = norm.cdf(-(SIGMA*(x-MU))) + norm.cdf(-(SIGMA*(x+MU)))
alpha_w = 2 * norm.cdf(-x)
R = alpha_t/alpha_w
